name: Alemannic German
notes:
Alemannic German (Schwyzerdütsch, Alsatian, Swabian, Vorarlbergisch), ISO 639-3 gsw. This is the DIALECT, not Schweizerhochdeutsch: the parent de-CH models Swiss Standard German, which is Standard German with Swiss features and shares the de-DE grapheme table. Alemannic diverges from that table systematically, and the divergences below are what this spec declares.

The High German consonant shift ran to completion, so ⟨ch⟩ is the Ach-Laut [x]~[χ] in every position, word-initially included (Chatz, Chilbi, Chueche), and the Standard German Ich-Laut [ç] is absent altogether; ⟨k⟩ and ⟨ck⟩ spell the affricate /kx/ (Brocki, Stock, Anke). There are no voiced obstruents: ⟨s⟩ is [s] in every position, and the lenis series is voiceless-unaspirated, transcribed either plainly or with a voicelessness ring. /r/ is an alveolar trill [r], and Standard German ⟨-er⟩ vocalisation to [ɐ] does not apply.

Spelling follows Dieth-Schreibung, where a doubled vowel letter marks length (Huus [huːs], Wii [viː], Füür [fyːr]) and ⟨y⟩/⟨yy⟩ traditionally stand for /iː/. A doubled consonant letter marks the preceding vowel short and, for the stops, spells the fortis rather than a geminate (Rugge [rukə]). The gold is split on how it writes that fortis — [k] in Rugge, a long lenis [ɡ̊ː] in seggle — so the ⟨gg⟩ entry costs a little PER against the second convention; the entry follows the description, not the majority notation.

Sources: Wikipedia, "Swiss German" (fortis/lenis, absence of voiced obstruents, /x/ without a [ç] allophone, ⟨k⟩/⟨ck⟩ = /kx/, alveolar-trill /r/, ⟨y⟩/⟨yy⟩ = /iː/); Wikipedia, "Alemannic German" (High and Highest Alemannic fricativize initial /k/ to [x]; these varieties use the Ach-Laut exclusively); de.wikipedia, "Dieth-Schreibung" (short vowels written singly, long vowels doubled). Russ (1994) and Haas (2000) are the standard descriptive references; editions not consulted.
